In summary, our research is concerned with
the modelling of a population of pancreatic islets and the description of the feed back control of the glucose–insulin dynamics.
the development of a mathematical model of the pancreatic islets that is able to reproduce the main observed features of the glucose/ insulin system.
the modelling of the pancreatic insulin secretion and its interaction with the glucose/insuline system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in silico, a single model can explain a large set of observed data.
the proposed model, which is able to reproduce a wide range of observed phenomena, provides a good description of pancreatic endocrine insulin secretion.
the proposed model provides a coherent explanation of a wide variety of phenomena observed experimentally.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed islet population model provides a simple, yet realistic, representation of the endocrine pancreatic system.

the model is a simple and effective tool for the simulation of the glucose/ insulin system, and that its simplicity and effectiveness are due to the fact that the system’s dynamics are the result of a large number (of the order of a million) of simple, independent, and randomly distributed controllers.

the islet population model proposed in this paper is a good candidate to explain a wide variety of phenomena observed in vivo, and may therefore be a useful tool for further in silico studies of the glucose/pancreatic insulin system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a population of independent islets with distributed reaction characteristics may explain the complex dynamics of glucose/insulin homeostasis, including the observed ultradian oscillations.

, in order for the model to reproduce the experimental data, it is necessary to have a large number of islets, all of which are characterized by a wide range of reaction times and sensitivities, and that the glucose–insulin dynamics are not linear.
a population model may be able to explain the observed oscillations of glucose and insulin in a way which cannot be achieved using a single islet model.
